text: In the last lesson a machine learned by turning two knobs until a line fitted some dots. A language model learns in the same way, yet it writes essays and code, so a great deal must sit between that line and this. This lesson is the map of what sits in between, so that whenever a lesson feels abstract, you can see where it leads.

The journey starts with mathematics, because every later idea is written in it. Linear algebra comes first. It treats a list of numbers as an arrow, and it treats a grid of numbers, called a matrix, as a machine that moves arrows around. Every word inside a model is such an arrow, and every layer of a model is mostly matrices acting on them.

Calculus comes next, because learning means nudging knobs downhill, and the derivative is what tells you which way is down, much as your feet feel the slope of a hill in the dark. Probability follows, because a model never states the next word with certainty. It hands out a share of belief to every possible word, and we need a fair way to score those beliefs.

With those tools we can study optimization, the craft of rolling downhill efficiently, and then classical machine learning, where models such as linear regression are small enough to understand completely. They are the training wheels of the course, since big ideas like overfitting appear there first, in a form you can see on a single plot.

Neural networks stack many simple layers, each a matrix followed by a gentle bend, and backpropagation is the bookkeeping that tells every knob in every layer which way to turn. You will write that bookkeeping yourself, as a small automatic differentiation engine, and then train real networks, including one that reads images of handwritten digits.

Then comes the destination. Text is cut into pieces called tokens, each token becomes a vector, and attention lets every word gather information from the words around it. Stack those blocks, train them to predict the next token, and you have a language model, which you will build in miniature as a small GPT of your own.

Every lesson pairs one idea with a short quiz and a problem you solve in code, and the problems build on one another, so the small functions you write now become the engine of that GPT later. Before the mathematics starts, though, we need its alphabet, so the next lesson is about reading notation: the sigma sign, subscripts and vectors.
